slides.title: Title
slides.notes: Open by making minimization geometric. A convex minimum is not only the lowest plotted point; it is where level sets stop shrinking and where the first-order certificate has no remaining descent direction. The lecture will keep existence and optimality separate so students can diagnose which part fails.

slides.title: Problem Shape
slides.notes: Separate two questions that are often conflated. The infimum is a number; a minimum is a point that reaches that number. Convexity gives strong structure, but it does not by itself guarantee attainment. The rest of the section explains which level-set and recession checks make attainment possible.

slides.title: Level Sets
slides.notes: Use sublevel sets as the existence picture. A minimizing sequence eventually lives in any level set just above the infimum. If one of those sets is closed and bounded in finite dimension, a convergent subsequence appears, and lower semicontinuity lets the limit inherit the minimum value.

slides.title: Zero Subgradient
slides.notes: Present zero subgradient as the optimality certificate, not merely a calculus slogan. For differentiable functions it is the familiar zero gradient condition. For nonsmooth convex functions, the whole subdifferential matters, and containing zero means every supporting affine lower bound is compatible with no descent direction.

slides.title: Recession Escape
slides.notes: Use recession to explain the main failure mode. A minimizing sequence can leave every bounded region even while objective values decrease. Sometimes this means the function is unbounded below; sometimes the value is approached but not attained. Either way, the level-set picture reveals why a compactness argument cannot start.

slides.title: Existence Checklist
slides.notes: Give students a practical existence checklist. Properness avoids meaningless values, closedness supports limits, bounded sublevel sets stop escape, and a finite infimum gives the target value. The theorem-level argument is compactness, but the slide makes clear which geometric failure each assumption prevents.

slides.title: Nonsmooth Minima
slides.notes: Use the absolute value shape to make nonsmooth optimality concrete. There is no single derivative at the corner, but there are many supporting slopes. Since the interval of subgradients includes zero, the corner satisfies the optimality certificate and no directional descent is possible.

slides.title: Numerical Checker
slides.notes: Tie this slide directly to the notebook invariant. The sampled minimizer should have both a low value and a small stationarity residual. The value test catches points that are stationary but not lowest in the sampled view, while the gradient or subgradient test catches points that still have a visible descent direction.

slides.title: Learner Lab
slides.notes: Frame the lab as a separation of existence from stationarity. Students should modify one term, inspect whether level sets still trap near-minimizers, and then compute the zero-gradient or zero-subgradient residual. A good explanation says whether the new behavior is a point minimum, a flat minimizer set, escape, or unboundedness.

slides.title: Recap
slides.notes: Close with the two-part checklist. Existence comes from trapping minimizing sequences with closed bounded level sets; optimality comes from zero belonging to the subdifferential. Recession analysis explains the important failures, so students should always ask which of these three mechanisms is doing the work.
